column4: The source section’s root ء ث ر is voiced here as the magicians refuse to prefer Pharaoh over the clear signs and their Creator; his power reaches only this worldly life, making their choice under threat a pointed counterpart to preferring it.
This is the source section’s exact pairing of خير and أبقى: the magicians end by naming God better and more enduring, after refusing Pharaoh’s worldly authority.
The source section’s two sides meet in one address: do not fix one’s eyes on the worldly life’s flower; the Lord’s provision is better and more enduring.
The source section’s warning about preferring the lowly worldly life is stated directly: this person “preferred the life of this world,” and the following ayah gives the destination.
The following ayah completes the worldly preference’s outcome by naming Hell as its abode, the negative side of the section’s choice between transient and enduring outcomes.
The other side of the passage is the one who fears standing before the Lord and restrains the self from desire, matching the section’s account of choosing the better rather than the lower impulse.
This ayah completes the other side of the choice: the Garden is the abode of the one who feared and restrained desire.

The source section names the root ء ث ر and this ayah uses its favoring sense: Joseph’s brothers say God preferred him over them, a concrete positive or bestowed preference beside the section’s condemned preference.

The source section explicitly links ء ث ر to favoring another over oneself: the Anṣār put the emigrants first even when needy, and the ayah calls these people successful, showing preference directed toward good.
The source section’s root ب ق ي joins “what remains” to good: in Shuʿayb’s market warning, what God leaves after honest dealing is better for the believers than illicit gain.
The source section develops ب ق ي as a remnant that still has goodness within it; this ayah calls for people of such a remnant who restrain corruption among earlier peoples.

The flood’s foam is carried away while what benefits people remains on earth. This gives the section’s discarded residue and lasting good a vivid parallel, with both a physical remainder and a moral distinction.
A rain-fed growth cycle ends with dry fragments scattered by the wind, closely staging the section’s pasture becoming worthless residue and the disappearance of worldly display.

The ayah calls wealth and children the adornment of worldly life, then says enduring righteous deeds are better in reward and hope; this is the section’s transient adornment versus lasting good in direct terms.

The source section’s root غ ث و appears for people struck down and made into refuse; here the debris image extends from withered growth to a destroyed people and warns against rejecting the messengers.
The source section’s root ب ق ي is given moral content as lasting righteous deeds, which are better with the Lord in reward and outcome.
This ayah states the section’s measure of permanence: what people possess runs out, while what is with God remains.
What people are given is described as enjoyment and adornment of worldly life, while what is with God is better and more lasting, the section’s distinction applied to possessions.
The ayah explicitly calls worldly provision enjoyment, then says what is with God is better and lasting for believers; it closely matches the section’s two sides.
The source section explicitly notes the contrary use of أبقى: here the punishment of the Hereafter is more severe and more lasting, so permanence itself does not make an outcome good.
The same Taha narrative says the criminal does not die or live in Hell, recalling the section’s image of suspended existence and bounding its promise of a lasting good with a lasting punishment.
Everything on earth is passing away, the temporal side of the section’s distinction; the next ayah names what remains.
The next ayah says the face of the Lord of majesty and honor remains, completing the preceding claim and giving the source section’s “God alone in permanence” idea a Qur’anic formulation.
The ayah says all things perish except His Face and that all return to Him, a direct formulation of the permanence singled out by the source section’s root ء ث ر branch about remaining alone.
Rain-fed plants flourish, then become cut stubble as if they had not flourished; this repeats the pasture-to-residue scene behind the section’s contrast of the passing and lasting.
Crops grow in varied colors, yellow, then become debris; this is another direct growth-to-waste scene that makes the section’s discarded residue concrete.
The ayah compares worldly life to rain-fed growth that pleases, yellows, and becomes debris, while warning that the world’s adornment and rivalry are only temporary enjoyment.

The source section’s verb of preferring is sharpened by this rebuke: the believers sought the immediate spoils, while God willed the Hereafter, making a worldly gain the wrong selection in its context.
The call directly challenges those content with worldly life instead of the Hereafter and calls worldly enjoyment little, closely matching the section’s rebuke of preferring the nearer life.
Worldly life is described as play and amusement, while the Hereafter’s abode is better for those mindful of God; this gives the section’s passing/lasting contrast a direct formulation.
The ayah names worldly enjoyment as little and says the Hereafter is better for the mindful, an explicit valuation of the two sides in the section.
The ayah condemns those who bought the life of this world at the price of the Hereafter, a concrete exchange of the better enduring outcome for the nearer one.
For one who desires the immediate life, God hastens what He wills in it, but the ayah then names Hell as the end; choosing the near reward does not secure lasting good.
The paired ayah describes one who desires the Hereafter, strives for it, and believes; the effort is accepted, setting the alternative choice beside the preceding worldly desire.
Those who desire worldly life and its adornment receive their deeds’ reward in this life, paralleling the section’s warning about choosing what passes.
The next ayah completes that worldly bargain: such people have nothing in the Hereafter but Fire, so their immediate reward leaves no enduring share.

After worldly desires are listed in the preceding ayah, this one offers something better: gardens, purified spouses, and God’s approval. It makes the section’s “better” concrete without treating worldly adornment as the final good.
The Prophet is told to turn from one who turns away from remembrance and wants only worldly life, directly joining the section’s preference for the world to avoidance of reminder.

When trade or amusement appears, people leave the Messenger standing; the ayah says what is with God is better than trade and amusement, a precise scene of choosing immediate display over a better provision.
Believers are described as people whom trade and sale do not distract from remembering God, prayer, and giving; this is the opposite ordering to the section’s preference for worldly life.
Believers are warned not to let wealth and children distract them from remembering God; those who do so are the losers, a specific account of the section’s condemned preference.
The speaker calls worldly life only a temporary enjoyment and the Hereafter the lasting home, directly articulating the section’s value distinction.
This ayah calls worldly life play and amusement and the Hereafter the true life, making the section’s contrast between temporary and enduring life explicit.
People know only the outward aspect of worldly life and are heedless of the Hereafter; this names the narrowed valuation that the section challenges.
The ayah says worldly adornment is only enjoyment of this life and that the Hereafter belongs to the mindful, connecting material display to the section’s temporary side.
The neighboring ayah says the worldly desirer’s knowledge reaches only that limit, completing the preceding warning about turning from remembrance for worldly life.
Before the market scene in the following ayah, the Friday call commands people to leave trade and hasten to God’s remembrance; the command makes the choice staged in 62:11 legible.
After prayer, people are permitted to disperse and seek God’s bounty; this completes the market passage and bounds its rebuke as a matter of priority, not a ban on livelihood.
Those who do not expect to meet God are content with worldly life and heedless of the signs; the following ayah names their abode, linking worldly preference with neglected guidance.
This ayah gives the abode of those described in 10:7 as Fire, completing the consequence of contentment with worldly life alone.
Those who trade worldly life for the Hereafter are promised a great reward whether they are killed or victorious, giving the section’s preference a concrete faithful form.
The ayah asks who desires the reward of this world, then says God holds reward of both this world and the Hereafter; it prevents reducing goodness to a single material reward.

The command to seek the Hereafter with what God has given while not forgetting one’s share of worldly life supplies a boundary: preferring the lasting good need not mean erasing ordinary worldly provision.
The person who gives and is mindful of God receives the promised easy path, beginning a passage where generosity rather than self-protective holding directs one’s choice.
Belief in the best promise completes the giver’s orientation in the preceding ayah, a choice directed toward an outcome beyond immediate possession.
The next ayah says God will ease this person toward ease, completing the positive consequence of giving and belief.
The passage’s opposite person is miserly, self-sufficient, and denying the best promise; that reversal makes the choice in the section concrete.
The next ayah completes the negative orientation as denial of the best promise, rather than merely having little wealth.
The miser is eased toward hardship, completing the two-sided outcome of the choices contrasted in 92:5–9.
The following ayah says the person’s wealth will not avail him when he falls, completing the passage’s distinction between possessions and lasting outcome.
Provision may be expanded or restricted, but people rejoice in worldly life although its enjoyment is little beside the Hereafter; abundance alone is not the section’s lasting good.
The ayah describes God distributing worldly livelihoods and ranks, then says the Lord’s mercy is better than what people accumulate, distinguishing provision from the greater good.
Wealth and children are called a trial, while a great reward is with God; the ayah clarifies why worldly goods cannot stand in for the good that remains.
Some ask only for good in worldly life and have no share in the Hereafter; this is the section’s condemned narrowing of what counts as a desirable outcome.
The neighboring supplication asks for good in both worlds and protection from the Fire, giving a balanced alternative to seeking only worldly good.
The next ayah says these people have a share from what they earned, completing the consequence of the balanced supplication.
The ayah stages the attractions of women, children, wealth, horses, cattle, and tilled land as worldly adornment; the next ayah offers what is better, making the object of preference concrete.
The question asks whether abundant wealth and children mean that good things are being hastened to people; it challenges the equation of worldly abundance with true good.
This ayah answers that such people do not perceive that the abundance may be a trial, completing the challenge to treat material plenty as the selected good.
The source section’s account of خير as good that is not refuse connects to the command not to choose the inferior for charity—something the giver would accept only with eyes closed.
The ayah says the bad and good are not equal even if abundance of the bad attracts; this sharpens the source section’s distinction between abundant-looking goods and genuinely good choice.
God will distinguish the impure from the pure; this supplies a sorting image for the section’s selected, refuse-free side, though the ayah’s main subject is testing believers.
The ayah says God separates the bad from the good and piles the bad together, a close sorting counterpart to the section’s image of leaving refuse aside.
This preceding ayah identifies the emigrants who were driven from their homes and seek God’s bounty; it completes the setting for the Anṣār’s preference in 59:9.
The ayah says God would not destroy towns while their people are reformers, completing 11:116’s call for a morally sustaining remnant with the consequence its presence can have.
The successful person is the one who purifies the soul, a specific inner counterpart to the section’s claim that the right choice selects what is good rather than refuse.
The neighboring ayah gives the opposite outcome to the one who buries the soul, completing the passage’s purification-versus-loss contrast.

The heirs to scripture seize the lowly, passing goods of this life while expecting forgiveness; this connects the source section’s low-value side to a specific choice of inferior gain over moral fidelity.
Here خير means property or an estate left behind, unlike “better” in the source section; that material sense matters because the section is weighing worldly property against enduring good.
The source section’s root خ ي ر also appears here in the sense of wealth: intense love of material good can pull a person toward the worldly side the section warns about.

The ayah uses خير for property one can spend and directs that spending toward relatives, orphans, and the needy, connecting the source section’s material sense of “good” to how possessions are put to good use.

People are deluded by worldly life and forget the meeting of this day; the root ن س ي named by the source section thus connects discarded remembrance with the consequence of preferring the passing life.
Those who turn away from God’s signs forget what their own hands have sent ahead; this makes the section’s forgetting image an act of neglect whose consequences remain.

Moses says his Lord neither errs nor forgets and that knowledge is in a record; this is a specific counter-image to forgetting, though the ayah speaks of divine knowledge rather than the Prophet’s recitation.
The people in punishment are told they forgot the meeting of this day and are now abandoned to it; what was treated as forgettable has persisted as their outcome.
The people are told they forgot the meeting of this day and are now forgotten, with Fire as their abode; this links worldly delusion to an afterlife consequence that cannot be discarded.
Those who forget God are made to forget themselves; this gives the section’s root ن س ي a moral reversal in which neglect of what matters destroys one’s own orientation.
The rebuke of commanding righteousness while forgetting oneself offers a concrete form of self-preference that contrasts with giving another priority, though it is not about the Hereafter explicitly.
One cannot reach righteousness until giving from what one loves; this makes the section’s contrast between self-reservation and a rightly directed preference concrete.
The Prophet is assured that the Hereafter is better for him than the first life, a concise formulation of the section’s valuation spoken as reassurance.
Every soul will taste death and worldly life is only delusive enjoyment; success is entering the Garden, grounding the section’s question of what truly counts as winning.
Those who claim only worldly life and death are corrected by the reminder that time does not erase accountability; this reverses the preference’s assumption that nothing remains.

After being created in the best form, the human can be brought low; this parallels the section’s contrast between high value and the lowly side of worldly preference, though the surah’s focus is human moral condition.
Whoever turns away from God’s remembrance is promised a constricted life and blindness at resurrection, a specific consequence for choosing heedlessness over reminder.
The person asks why he is raised blind though he once saw, introducing the next ayah’s link between neglect and being forgotten.
The answer says the person forgot God’s signs and is forgotten today; this completes the reversal between what was neglected and what remains at judgment.
The source section defines choosing as seeking and doing what is better; this ayah says God creates and chooses, shifting the act of choosing to the Creator and bounding human preference.
The ayah notes differences in worldly rank but says the Hereafter has greater degrees and excellence, distinguishing visible worldly status from the fuller scale of value.
Wealth and children are a trial and a great reward is with God, clarifying that things desired in worldly life test rather than guarantee good.
